atoms.text: The forced move: a player must act and every legal action worsens their position, so the rules themselves become the enemy.
The obligation to move: turn order cannot be passed, so waiting is forbidden and patience is impossible.
The winning trap: a superior player maneuvers the opponent into having only bad options, so victory is achieved without a direct attack.
The endgame: zugzwang appears when few pieces remain, so the story's crisis arrives after the world has been stripped down.
The reciprocal zugzwang: both players would prefer not to move, so whoever is forced to act loses.
The zugzwang symbol: a position is marked with a special notation, so a narrative can flag the exact moment agency becomes a burden.
The chess clock: time pressure forces decisions before analysis is complete, so deliberation is a luxury.
The pawn that must advance: a lowly piece is compelled forward and opens a fatal line, so the weakest actor triggers the collapse.
The stalemate avoided: a player escapes a draw by creating a forced-move position, so the story's resolution requires making the opponent act.
The negotiation with no walk-away: both parties must respond and every response concedes something, so the deal is a trap.
The inherited position: a character is born into a board they did not set up, so responsibility precedes choice.
The move that changes the outcome from win to loss: a single legal action flips the result, so the story can hinge on one decision.
The opponent who waits: a rival refuses to engage and lets the rules force action, so passivity is a strategy.
The ancient endgame study: the position was known for centuries before it was named, so the story can use forgotten knowledge as a weapon.
The player who sees it coming: an expert recognizes the trap before it closes, so the drama is in the impossibility of avoidance.
The game that is also a life: a character treats every social interaction as a board position, so paranoia is a system of analysis.
